name: Automated License Plate Readers (ALPR)
overview: ALPR systems capture images of passing vehicles and use optical character recognition to extract license plate characters. A detection may be associated with a timestamp, camera identifier, vehicle description, and location.
how: A camera captures a vehicle image; software locates the plate and interprets its characters; authorized users may search stored detections or receive alerts based on configured watchlists. Capabilities and retention depend on vendor and agency configuration.
collects: Search activity and alerts, depending on system
limits: Plate recognition can be inaccurate, especially with obscured or unusual plates.
A detection does not establish who was driving or why a vehicle was present.
Retention, data-sharing and access vary by agency and contract.
privacy: Read local policies and request retention, access, sharing and audit documentation.
For lawful protest travel, consider the privacy implications of travel records and plan using lawful transport choices.
Do not obstruct, alter, damage, or interfere with cameras or plates.
oversight: What is the retention period and who can change it?
Which agencies and vendors can search the data?
Are searches logged and independently audited?
What are the correction and challenge procedures?

name: CCTV and Video Analytics
overview: Video surveillance systems capture and store footage from fixed or mobile cameras. Analytics can detect objects or events, depending on configuration.
how: Cameras send video to recorders or hosted platforms. Authorized operators may view footage and apply search or detection tools.
collects: Camera location and field of view
limits: Video quality and lighting affect reliability.
An observed person or object may be misidentified.
A camera's presence does not prove that facial recognition is enabled.
privacy: Understand posted camera notices and public agency policies.
Use ordinary device privacy and account security practices.
Document surveillance concerns from a safe public place without interfering with equipment.
oversight: Who can view recordings?
How long are recordings retained?
Is analytics enabled, and for what purposes?
What independent audits exist?

sources.title: NIST — Video surveillance and image analysis research

name: Facial Recognition
overview: Facial recognition software compares facial features in images against other images or databases. Its accuracy and deployment rules vary.
how: Software detects a face, computes a numerical representation, and compares it against a reference collection; results are similarity scores, not automatic proof of identity.
limits: Performance varies with image quality and demographics.
A match should not substitute for independent investigation.
privacy: Review photo-sharing and account privacy settings.
Ask agencies whether facial recognition is used and how matches are verified.
Seek legal support if you believe a false match caused harm.
oversight: Is independent human review mandatory?
Which databases are searched?
How are error rates evaluated?
What appeal and correction processes exist?

name: Uncrewed Aerial Surveillance
overview: Drones can carry visible-light, thermal, or other sensors and may be used to observe areas from the air.
how: Operators fly remotely piloted aircraft and receive sensor data. Recording, zoom, and tracking capabilities depend on the aircraft and payload.
limits: Flight endurance, weather and visibility constrain coverage.
Thermal images do not reveal precise identity or intent.
A drone overhead does not establish that it is recording.
privacy: Check published agency drone-use policies and flight transparency reports.
Keep a safe distance and do not interfere with aircraft.
Record concerns through official complaint or public records channels.
oversight: Which missions are authorized?
Is a warrant required for particular uses?
What imagery is retained and shared?
Are flights and complaints logged?

name: Cell-Site Simulators
overview: Cell-site simulators imitate aspects of cellular infrastructure to obtain certain cellular device identifiers or signaling information, depending on technology and legal authority.
how: A simulator interacts with compatible nearby mobile devices at the radio-protocol level. Specific capabilities vary and should not be assumed from a product name.
collects: Potential device identifiers or signaling metadata
Other data only where supported and authorized
limits: Capabilities vary by cellular generation and deployment.
Presence and operation are not generally publicly verifiable.
Ordinary phone apps cannot reliably prove or rule out use.
privacy: Keep devices and operating systems updated.
Use end-to-end encrypted messaging for sensitive lawful communications; it does not conceal all metadata.
Consult qualified counsel and digital security organizations for situation-specific advice.
oversight: What legal process authorizes use?
What minimization and deletion rules apply?
Are bystander data and audits documented?
What disclosures are made to courts?

name: Social Media Monitoring
overview: Monitoring platforms collect or analyze public online posts and other available information to identify topics, trends, or accounts.
how: Software searches public content, extracts entities and patterns, and may link records across platforms. Some tools use automated classification.
collects: Timestamps, locations or hashtags where shared
limits: Online identity and intent are often uncertain.
Automated sentiment and association models can be misleading.
Private messages are not necessarily accessible to these tools.
privacy: Review account visibility, location tagging, and application permissions.
Use strong authentication and separate personal information from public advocacy where appropriate.
Verify claims before sharing protest-related information.
oversight: Which platforms and data brokers are used?
Are political or protected activities monitored?
What are the retention and deletion policies?
How are inaccurate classifications challenged?
